sections.heading: A.1 Conversions
sections.text: We would like to make a few conversions explicit that are obvious to optical astronomers — including at least one of the authors — but proved difficult for another of the authors to track down and understand. We do this with the aim of improving communication between scientists from different fields, who often use different vocabulary and units to discuss the same properties. For converting between magnitude and flux in our simulations, we assume a zeropoint ZP of 25, appropriate for ZTF. The explicit conversion between flux F F and magnitude m m with ZP = 25 \mathrm{ZP}=25 is F = 10 − ( m − 25 ) / 2.5 ⟷ m = 25 − 2.5 log 10 F . \displaystyle F=10^{-(m-25)/2.5}\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad m=25-2.5\log_{10}F. (4) F F is therefore a scaled flux, without physical units. It only has meaning with a known zeropoint, or for comparisons with other scaled fluxes using the same zeropoint. The ZTF IPAC server generally returns fluxes in units of digital number DN. The conversion between flux in units of DN and flux in units of Jy (or, more precisely, the specific flux density F ν F_{\nu} ) is (e.g, Eq. 9 of West (2021) ) F [ Jy ] = F [ DN ] × 10 ( 8.9 − ZPmag DN ) / 2.5 \displaystyle F_{\mathrm{[Jy]}}=F_{\mathrm{[DN]}}\times 10^{(8.9-\mathrm{ZPmag_{DN}})/2.5} (5) where F [ DN ] F_{\mathrm{[DN]}} is the quantity forcediffimflux and ZPmag DN \mathrm{ZPmag_{DN}} is zpdiff .

sections.heading: A.2 Sky noise for simulations
sections.text: Figure 14 : Skynoise σ sky \sigma_{\mathrm{sky}} as an input to the SN simulations, derived for the g g and r r bands separately from ZTF data. For all of our simulated SNe, we drew δ sky \delta_{\mathrm{sky}} from a skew normal fit to all visits pertaining to a specific sky position in a given field. Here, we show 50 sample fits as well an example distribution for the g g and r r bands separately. Sky noise is an input for realize_lcs() that quantifies the background noise. In realize_lcs() the skynoise σ sky \sigma_{\mathrm{sky}} combines with the the uncertainty the photon counts in quadrature: σ F = σ sky 2 + F \displaystyle\sigma_{F}=\sqrt{\sigma_{\mathrm{sky}}^{2}+F} (6) where F F is the photon counts flux and σ F \sigma_{F} is the total uncertainty on the flux. σ sky \sigma_{\mathrm{sky}} describes the total noise due to observing conditions; for a given sky position, this includes both constant effects (such as the general sky brightness in that region) as well as temporary effects (such as the atmospheric conditions during a particular observation). We determined σ sky \sigma_{\mathrm{sky}} from the IPAC forced photometry server ( Masci et al. 2019 ; Masci et al. 2023 ) for the 212 ZTF SNe discussed in Sec. 5.1 , and calculated σ sky \sigma_{\mathrm{sky}} using σ sky = 10 0.4 × ( zpdiff − diffmaglim ) 5 \displaystyle\sigma_{\mathrm{sky}}=\frac{10^{0.4\times(\texttt{zpdiff}-\texttt{diffmaglim})}}{5} (7) where zpdiff is the photometric zeropoint and diffmaglim the magnitude limit for the difference image, as in Eq. 1 of Amenouche et al. (2025) . For each band and field, we fit the distribution of σ sky \sigma_{\mathrm{sky}} with a skew normal distribution for a total of 245 g g -band fits and 247 r r -band fits. (This is more than the number of SNe because some SNe appeared in multiple fields.) A sample of 50 random fits as well as an example distribution is shown in Fig. 14 for the g g and r r bands separately. In general, the σ sky \sigma_{\mathrm{sky}} distributions in g g peak at smaller values than in r r but have longer tails. For any SN simulation in a given band, we drew the skynoise for each observation from a randomly chosen skew normal fit for that band. Since we ran our searches on the g g - and r r -band simulations independently, we did not require that the fits be drawn from the same field. Note that Eq. A.2 can be inverted to solve for the flux F F when σ sky \sigma_{\mathrm{sky}} and σ F \sigma_{F} are known. This is important because sncosmo returns flux points F SN F_{\mathrm{SN}} that have already been randomly redrawn from a one-dimensional Gaussian with a width of σ F S ​ N \sigma_{F_{SN}} , whereas we want the option to add rebrightening and oscillation features to the template flux before calculating uncertainty. Therefore, for our simulations, we inverted Eq. A.2 to calculate the interpolated template flux F SN F_{\mathrm{SN}} given the reported σ F \sigma_{F} and the input σ sky \sigma_{\mathrm{sky}} , and then added the flux due to the rebrightening F rebr F_{\mathrm{rebr}} and oscillation features F osc F_{\mathrm{osc}} when necessary so that F = F SN + F rebr + F osc F=F_{\mathrm{SN}}+F_{\mathrm{rebr}}+F_{\mathrm{osc}} . We then calculated the overall uncertainty σ F \sigma_{F} with the new total flux F F , and redrew F F from the Gaussian with the width σ F \sigma_{F} .

sections.heading: A.3 More explorations of recoverable signals
sections.text: Figure 15 : 2D histogram showing f recov f_{\mathrm{recov}} across the range of f osc f_{\mathrm{osc}} for the basic search with λ = 1 \lambda=1 starting at t 0 + 20 t_{0}+20 d. In addition to the set of signals with f recov ≈ f osc f_{\mathrm{recov}}\approx f_{\mathrm{osc}} , the sets of aliased signals that correspond to Eq. 2 with n < 0 n<0 are annotated. These are equivalent to the ones highlighted in Eq. 3 . The gray shaded regions around the aliased signal sets depict the f recov = f osc ± 0.0021 f_{\mathrm{recov}}=f_{\mathrm{osc}}\pm 0.0021 definition. Our definition for a recoverable signal is a criterion on f LS f_{\mathrm{LS}} . Fig. 15 shows a 2D histogram of the frequencies f recov f_{\mathrm{recov}} associated with the periodogram peaks P max P_{\mathrm{max}} , compared to the simulated frequency f osc f_{\mathrm{osc}} , for the standard search ( λ = 1 \lambda=1 , starting at t 0 + 20 t_{0}+20 d). The recovery condition of both the signals around f recov = f osc f_{\mathrm{recov}}=f_{\mathrm{osc}} and the aliased signals described in Eq. 3 are better defined in frequency space, as f recov = f osc ± 0.0021 f_{\mathrm{recov}}=f_{\mathrm{osc}}\pm 0.0021 d -1 (or, for the aliased signals, around an alias of f osc f_{\mathrm{osc}} ); i.e., the recovered frequency is within 4.2 LS gridpoints Δ ​ f LS \Delta f_{\mathrm{LS}} of the simulated frequency. The choice of 4.2 gridpoints well captures the spread around T recov = T osc T_{\mathrm{recov}}=T_{\mathrm{osc}} for large T osc T_{\mathrm{osc}} , as seen in Fig. 4 , without being too restrictive. The choice of 4.2 as opposed to exactly 4 gridpoints is to take into account differences due to rounding. Figure 16 : Comparing fraction of recoverable signals for g g - (closed circles) and r r -band (open squares) simulations, across different values of λ \lambda and the spline fit start day, for T osc ≤ 50 T_{\mathrm{osc}}\leq 50 d (top) and T osc > 50 T_{\mathrm{osc}}>50 d (bottom). Fewer signals are recovered with the r r -band simulations, especially for shorter period signals and using λ = 10 \lambda=10 . The recoverability for the r r and g g bands are compared in Fig. 16 . The fraction recovered in the r r band is consistently worse than in the g g band, with the difference being at most 5% (for λ = 10 \lambda=10 and short period signals). This suggests that the r r -band lightcurves vary more rapidly for the templates we are using, which obscures the underlying oscillations. Both the rebrightening and oscillating features of SN 2022jli are attributed to accretion of the binary companion, although it is unclear how universal they are. However, for our standard search, the rebrightening features do not have any effect on how | f recov − f osc | \left|f_{\mathrm{recov}}-f_{\mathrm{osc}}\right| is distributed (Fig. 17 ), suggesting that our search with λ = 1 \lambda=1 is robust to the kinds of rebrightening features found in SN 2022jli. Figure 17 : The difference in recovered versus true frequency as a function of the rebrightening parameters for the simulated SNe. None of the five rebrightening parameters has a strong effect on the signal recovery for λ = 1 \lambda=1 .

sections.heading: A.4 Non-symmetric oscillations
sections.text: Figure 18 : Like Fig. 15 but for the skewed sawtooth oscillations rather than symmetric sinusoids. The sawtooth functions have a ratio of rise time to fall time of 1:4 (i.e., they take four times as long to decay as to rise). The x x axis is limited to [ 0 , 0.16 ] [0,0.16] in order to highlight the new feature: besides the overdensity around f recov = f osc f_{\mathrm{recov}}=f_{\mathrm{osc}} , there is an additional overdensity at f recov = 2 ​ f osc f_{\mathrm{recov}}=2f_{\mathrm{osc}} , particularly for longer period signals ( f osc < 0.03 f_{\mathrm{osc}}<0.03 d), leading to a 5% reduction in the number of signals recoverable around f osc f_{\mathrm{osc}} or an alias. While the oscillations for SN 2022esa were symmetric ( Maeda et al. 2026 ) , the oscillations for SN 2022jli were skewed with shorter rise times than fall times ( Chen et al. 2024 ) . If the periodic oscillations are skewed, this means that some power will instead be present at higher order frequencies, so that our sensitivity to real signals would decrease. To test this, we resimulated the 10 000 SN lightcurves with the periodic oscillations being skewed sawtooth functions rather than symmetric sinusoids, keeping all other parameters such as the period the same. For the sawtooth functions, we set the fall time to be four times as long as the rise time, similar to what was seen for SN 2022jli ( Chen et al. 2024 ) . As Fig. 18 shows, when compared to the equivalent search on symmetric sinusoidal oscillations as depicted in Fig. 15 , there is an additional overdensity of signals recovered at f recov = 2 ​ f osc f_{\mathrm{recov}}=2f_{\mathrm{osc}} . This is especially true for the longer period signals (the left side of the figure). Overall, this reduces the number of recoverable signals by 5% for both the λ = 1 \lambda=1 and λ = 10 \lambda=10 searches as there is less power in the periodogram at frequencies around f osc f_{\mathrm{osc}} and its aliases. If we additionally consider the first higher order mode by including signals recovered at f recov = 2 ​ f osc f_{\mathrm{recov}}=2f_{\mathrm{osc}} and its aliases, the missing 5% of signals are mostly recovered but at much lower P max P_{\mathrm{max}} values.

sections.heading: A.5 Search grids with smaller T LS min T^{\mathrm{min}}_{\mathrm{LS}}
sections.text: When using our standard periodogram grid with T min LS = 6 T^{\mathrm{LS}}_{\mathrm{min}}=6 d, we can stillrecover signals with T osc < 6 T_{\mathrm{osc}}<6 d via their longer period aliases. Alternatively, we can also use search grids that extend down to shorter periods to potentially increase our sensitivity to shorter oscillations, and accept that some longer period signals will be recovered by their shorter period aliases: T recov = ( 1 T osc − n ​ δ ​ f obs ) − 1 \displaystyle T_{\mathrm{recov}}=\left(\frac{1}{T_{\mathrm{osc}}}-n\delta f_{\mathrm{obs}}\right)^{-1} (8) (e.g., Eq. 45 in VanderPlas (2018) 6 6 6 See footnote associated with Eq. 8 on the choice of sign convention. ). An example of this concept is shown in Fig. 19 . To explore this, we also tried search grids with T LS min T_{\mathrm{LS}}^{\mathrm{min}} of three days and one days. The search results for T min LS = 1 T^{\mathrm{LS}}_{\mathrm{min}}=1 d are shown in Fig. 20 , to help visualize the signals that are recovered at aliased frequencies. Overall, the three periodogram grids recovered similar numbers of signals (Fig. 21 ) for both λ = 1 \lambda=1 and λ = 10 \lambda=10 , although more of these are recovered at their aliased frequencies for T LS min = 3 T_{\mathrm{LS}}^{\mathrm{min}}=3 d and 1 d. Interestingly, the search grids with smaller T LS min T_{\mathrm{LS}}^{\mathrm{min}} do not recover any additional short period signals compared to the grid with T LS min = 6 T_{\mathrm{LS}}^{\mathrm{min}}=6 d, indicating that the short period signals are efficiently recovered at their aliased frequencies. We therefore find no benefit in using search grids with smaller values of T LS min T_{\mathrm{LS}}^{\mathrm{min}} . Figure 19 : Lightcurve and spline fit (left), residuals (middle), and periodogram (right) for an example simulation with T osc = 20 T_{\mathrm{osc}}=20 d and a three-day cadence. The periodogram shows the reflected regions beyond T LS min < 6 T_{\mathrm{LS}}^{\mathrm{min}}<6 d, including the aliased (i.e., reflected) versions of the signals at higher frequencies. Fluctuations determine the relative heights of the peaks, so that f recov f_{\mathrm{recov}} could be at either the main frequency f osc f_{\mathrm{osc}} or one of the aliased frequencies. Figure 20 : Same as Fig. 15 but using the periodogram grid with T LS min = 1 T_{\mathrm{LS}}^{\mathrm{min}}=1 d. (The figure is compressed in the vertical direction so the lines are at different angles compared to the previous figure.) The search grid is six times as large as the one with T LS min = 6 T_{\mathrm{LS}}^{\mathrm{min}}=6 d, and the plot itself can be seen as the one in Fig. 15 reflected six times over the vertical axis. This shows the additional aliases that appear when using a grid with T LS min T_{\mathrm{LS}}^{\mathrm{min}} less than twice the cadence. Figure 21 : Signal recoverability as a function of T osc T_{\mathrm{osc}} for periodogram grids with values of T LS min T_{\mathrm{LS}}^{\mathrm{min}} , for the λ = 1 \lambda=1 (left) and λ = 10 \lambda=10 (right) spline fits. There is no major difference between the total number of recoverable signals for the three choices of periodogram grid, although larger fractions are recoverable only at their aliased frequencies with the smaller values of T LS min T_{\mathrm{LS}}^{\mathrm{min}} . Vertical error bars show counting uncertainties.

sections.heading: A.6 Using only stripped envelope SN templates
sections.text: In our main search, we have included all CC SN templates available in sncosmo . However, this also encompasses many SNe that are classified as non-stripped envelope SNe, including some with less well behaved lightcurves, and in principle using only stripped envelope SN templates could produce a better and more targeted result. To explore this, we reran the λ = 1 \lambda=1 and λ = 10 \lambda=10 searches on a new set of 10 000 SNe simulations that only included the Ib, Ic, and IIb templates, as well as their subtypes such as Ic-BL. The searches started t 0 + 20 t_{0}+20 d and ran on the simulated lightcurves with the standard three-day cadence and 200-day observation period, using the periodogram grid with T LS min = 6 T_{\mathrm{LS}}^{\mathrm{min}}=6 d. We find that, when only using the stripped envelope SN templates, the recovered SNe increase by less than a percent for the λ = 1 \lambda=1 search and 3.5% for the λ = 10 \lambda=10 search. Figure 22 shows this comparison when using the more limited set of templates versus the whole set of core collapse SN templaets. The false alarm fractions are also not strongly affected by these different set of templates. Figure 22 : Comparing the false alarm and true acceptance fractions at different P max P_{\mathrm{max}} thresholds when simulating the SNe only from the templates of stripped envelope SNe. The λ = 1 \lambda=1 (solid curves) and λ = 10 \lambda=10 (dashed curves) searches both start at t 0 + 20 t_{0}+20 d. The equivalent quantities for the simulations that include all SN templates are plotted as the semitransparent curves. Using a more limited set of templates does not result in a big difference in either the signal recovery or the noise rejection. Figure 23 : The effects of randomly dropping 10% of observations is a minimal loss of 1% of detectable signals, while randomly dropping 30% of observations reduces the detectable percentage by 5%. Figure 24 : Similar to Fig. 8 but with the two- (top) or seven-day cadence (bottom) observations, compared to our standard three-day cadence assumption.

sections.heading: A.7 Properties of the ZTF-detected SNe
sections.text: Figure 25 : The mean (circle) and standard deviation (bars) in the days since the previous visit, for all SNe in our moderately bright ZTF sample, split into the g g (green) and r r (red) bands. The vertical axis shows increasing time, from bottom to top, and each point corresponds to a single field in a given SN; since some SNe were present in multiple fields, there are more points than there are SNe. The standard three- and two-day cadences of the public surveys (left) are visible, while the private programs (right) often include multiple observations a night. For the data plotted here, fields with IDs >1000 (i.e., the secondary field grid) were removed but no other cleaning was performed. Some SNe included visits from both public and private programs. The ZTF data we used included visits from both the public and private programs. While the public programs had standard three- and two-day cadences, the private program included both higher (i.e., multiple observations per night) and lower cadences. The mean and standard deviation in the days since the last visit for any given field are plotted in Fig. 25 for the moderately bright sample, and the difference in cadence between the public and private surveys can clearly be seen, as well as the switch from the three- to two-day public surveys. For the moderate ZTF sample, we drew the simulated SNe from a redshift range [ 0.03 , 0.06 ] [0.03,0.06] to match the range of the real SNe, and the scaling parameter from the range [ 10 − 16 , 5 × 10 − 15 ] [10^{-16},5\times 10^{-15}] to produce a similar set of peak brightnesses as the real sample. For the bright and nearby sample, we used a redshift range of [ 0.001 , 0.03 ] [0.001,0.03] and a narrow scaling parameter range [ 2 × 10 − 14 , 3 × 10 − 14 ] [2\times 10^{-14},3\times 10^{-14}] , again to match the peak brightness distribution of the real sample. Figure 26 : P max P_{\mathrm{max}} vs. the number of data points included in the spline fit N obs N_{\mathrm{obs}} for the g g and r r bands individually, for the nearby and very bright ZTF SN sample, with the results from 10 000 simulations shown in the gray 2D histogram in the background (logarithmic scaling). The outlier SNe are labeled; all can be discarded after visual inspection of the lightcurves and spline fits. The only SN that appears in both the g g - and r r -band plots, SN 2018hna, was covered by multiple fields explaining both the large N obs N_{\mathrm{obs}} as well as the P max P_{\mathrm{max}} outlier due to the resultant poor spline fit. Figure 27 : Examples of SN lightcurves, spline fits, and periodograms for the nearby ZTF sample. These six periodogram outliers can all be excluded as real signal candidates. SN 2018hna, the only g g -band outlier, appeared as a periodogram outlier in both the g g and r r bands due to its position being present in multiple fields. Of the others, SNs 2019iex and 2022prv demonstrate the limitation of the spline fit, which was tuned to a moderate bright sample and cannot accommodate the larger changes in slope and short-term variability (both real and instrumental) more frequently present in brighter lightcurves.

Zhu , † † thanks: Corresponding author: sylvia.zhu@desy.de Affiliation: Deutsches Elektronen-Synchrotron (DESY), Platanenallee 6, D-15738 Zeuthen, Germany Jakob Nordin Affiliation: Institut für Physik, Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, D-12489 Berlin, Germany Emma de Oña-Wilhelmi Affiliation: Deutsches Elektronen-Synchrotron (DESY), Platanenallee 6, D-15738 Zeuthen, Germany Andrea Ercolino Affiliation: Argelander Institut für Astronomie, Auf dem Hügel 71, DE-53121 Bonn, Germany Received August 3, 2026 Abstract Context. Stripped envelope supernovae occur in massive stars that have lost their outer layers before exploding, possibly from binary interactions. Recently, SN 2022jli was detected with significant periodic oscillations in its lightcurve, likely due to accretion from a binary companion onto the newborn compact object. Aims. While evidence for periodic oscillations has been found in a few bright and noteworthy supernovae, the population properties are best understood with systematic searches of large data sets. We present prospects for running a search on data from ZTF and similar surveys that is flexible and computationally inexpensive, with the goal of setting up a search in realtime on data from ZTF, LSST, and similar surveys. Methods. We simulate core collapse supernova lightcurves with additional features from the binary interactions. We use spline fits to remove the underlying supernova behavior and isolate the periodicities, then apply a Lomb-Scargle periodogram to recover the simulated period. By varying the conditions, we can make recommendations for different kinds of data sets. Finally, we run the search on two sets of archival ZTF supernovae to illustrate the concept. Results. For a wide range of binary interaction parameters, we find that a long baseline (200 days) of observations with a three-day cadence effectively retrieve ≈ \approx 50% of the binary oscillations. However, this rate plummets with more typical observation durations; only a few percent are recoverable with a 30-day observation, and 10% with a 75-day observation. A substantial fraction of supernovae could therefore have binary companion interactions that have simply been undetected. Out of 212 moderately bright and well observed ZTF supernovae, we find suggestions of periodic oscillations in two candidates. Key Words. supernovae: general – binaries: general – accretion 1 Introduction Stars with masses ≳ 10 ​ M ⊙ \gtrsim\!10\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot} end their lives as core collapse (CC) supernovae (SNe). Based on their spectra, they are categorized as a subtype of either type I (no hydrogen lines) or type II (hydrogen lines) SNe. The CC SNe classified as type I are also referred to as stripped envelope SNe, along with the type IIb (weak hydrogen lines), as the lack of hydrogen and sometimes helium lines indicates that the outer layer has been depleted before explosion ( Filippenko, 1997 ) . The progenitors of stripped envelope SNe could be single massive stars with strong stellar winds, or massive stars in binaries that have lost their envelopes due to binary interactions ( Conti, 1975 ; Conti, 1996 ; Podsiadlowski et al., 1992 ) (see also Jerkstrand et al., 2026 , for a recent review) . In fact, the majority of stars with masses above a few M ⊙ are known to exist in multiple star systems (e.g., Fig. 1 of Offner et al. (2023) ), and simulations indicate that over half of stripped envelope SNe come from massive stars in binary systems ( Kochanek, 2009 ; Zapartas et al., 2017 ; Zapartas et al., 2026 ) . Late-time images of CC SNe have uncovered five binary companions to date ( Zapartas et al., 2026 , and references therein) . Some of the SN themselves should also show evidence of binary interactions. This was seen in SN 2022jli, a type Ic at a distance of 23 Mpc ( Moore et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) : After the initial decline, the SN then rebrightened approximately 50 days after detection and reached a secondary peak as bright as the initial brightness at detection. It also showed strong periodic oscillations with a period of 12 days during this rebrightening episode, which lasted for around 200 days. In the binary scenario, the SN shock disturbs the companion’s outer layers and causes them to inflate. The newborn compact object then accretes this inflated material, resulting in both the rebrightening and periodic oscillations ( Hirai et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2025 ; King and Lasota, 2024 ) . In addition, shifts in the velocities of the H α \alpha ( Chen et al., 2024 ) and Pa β \beta ( Cartier et al., 2026 ) lines were discovered that were consistent with the orbital modulation deduced from the periodic oscillations. This all paints a picture of accretion from a binary companion as opposed to interactions between the supernova shock and overdensities in the circumstellar environment, an alternative explanation for short-term variability in SN lightcurves ( Nagao et al., 2026 , e.g.,) . The nature of the newborn compact object is unknown, although the supernova brightness and presumed strength of the natal kick suggest a neutron star is more likely than a black hole. In the case of a neutron star, a magnetar engine would provide enough energy to explain the rebrightening but not the lightcurve oscillations or the hydrogen line velocity shifts ( Orellana et al., 2025 ; Cartier et al., 2026 ) . Additionally, evidence for a gamma-ray excess at 1 GeV starting half a year after the initial SN was reported by Chen et al. (2024) and Zhang et al. (2025) , wit the gamma-ray arrival times being potentially consistent with the 12.4-day periodicity. Any gamma-ray excess could be due to either an accretion-powered relativistic jet or a magnetar central engine ( Hirai et al., 2025 ) , and the six-month delay caused by the region’s initially high opacity to gamma rays. A few other candidates for periodic lightcurve oscillations have been reported. Most prominently, a 32-day period was found in SN 2022esa ( Maeda et al., 2026 ) , a type Ic-CSM at a distance of around 100 Mpc. For this SN, the oscillations began immediately after the start of the main SN peak, and there was no rebrightening episode. The authors interpret the data as being more consistent with circumstellar material interaction, although they do not rule out a binary companion origin. An 8.4-day periodicity was also reported for SN 2015ap ( Ragosta et al., 2025 ) . The observed lightcurve modulations in SN 2022jli, SN2022esa, and SN2015ap may arise from the interaction between a newly born compact object and a companion star ( Hirai et al., 2025 ; Ercolino et al., 2026 ) while in other transients, especially superluminous supernovae, these undulations might instead be related to precession effects from a magnetar central engine ( Mashhoon et al., 1984 ; Hosseinzadeh et al., 2022 ; Farah et al., 2026 ) . Massive stars in binaries tend to explode at particularly small orbital separations from their companions ( Sana et al., 2012 ) . If these binaries remain bound after the SN explosion, they could evolve into a class of accreting binary ( King, 1988 ; Shao and Li, 2015 ) . If the companion is also sufficiently massive to undergo a supernova explosion, the compact objects could eventually merge to produce the gravitational-wave signals that have been detected by LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA ( The LIGO Scientific Collaboration et al., 2026 ) . Observations of more SN 2022jli-like systems would shed light on the evolution of massive stars in binaries. However, the few such SNe found so far have been particularly bright and/or well observed, and so are not necessarily representative of the average SN. To better understand the population of such systems, it is important to search for evidence of them systematically. We present prospects for systematically searching for periodicities in CC SNe lightcurves, using the Zwicky Transient Facility ( Bellm et al., 2019 , ZTF,) as our reference observatory. In our simulations, we focus on simulating lightcurves that would cover a large parameter space of observational properties. We explore how to set up a broad search to identify potentially interesting candidates, which could then be followed up with further observations and/or examined with a more tailored approach. Our findings can be used to inform search setups under more general conditions. We describe our choices for the simulated SN lightcurves and binary interaction parameters in Sec. 2 and the search procedure development, such as the choice of spline fit and periodogram grid, in Sec. 3 . We then discuss some results when applying various realistic observing conditions in Sec. 4 . In Sec. 5 we run our search on two sets of ZTF SNe as well as a few known SNe with periodic oscillations. Finally, we discuss our findings and prospects for future searches in Sec. 6 . 2 Simulations For the supernova lightcurves, we used the realize_lcs() function in sncosmo ( Barbary et al., 2025 ) . We simulated 10 000 SN lightcurves with additional binary-induced features to characterize the potential search sensitivity to a wide range of binary parameters. After simulating the lightcurves, we applied a spline fit to subtract out the underlying supernova behavior and a Lomb-Scargle periodogram on the residuals to isolate periodic signals, which will be discussed fully in Sec. 3 . We used SN 2022jli as a guideline but did not adhere too tightly to its properties to avoid biasing our simulations with a single example. For reference, SN 2022jli had a peak g g -band magnitude of around 15, equivalent to a scaled flux of 10 4 10^{4} assuming a zeropoint magnitude ZP = 25 \mathrm{ZP}=25 (Sec. A.1 ). The oscillations had a period of 12.4 days and an amplitude of around 10% in flux. The SN rebrightened 20 days after detection. The oscillations were significantly detected only after the rebrightening peak ( Moore et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) . We performed the simulations and searches in the ZTF g g and r r bands separately, as the relative cadence of observations in the two bands varies, and combining the results can be nontrivial if the color is changing. In the following sections, we focus on the g g -band results and report r r -band results when they differ. 2.1 Supernovae We generated the base SNe with a wide variety of SN templates. While the generalized version of the Lomb-Scargle periodogram can account for a non-zero mean, it still assumes a constant offset and cannot account for more complex behavior. These limits are longer than the periods of known X-ray binaries, which range from sub-hours to tens of days, and which are the later evolutionary stages of our systems. Indeed, Ercolino et al. The oscillations detected in SN 2022jli were skewed rather than symmetric ( Moore et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) , likely due to the orbital eccentricity caused by the compact object’s natal kick ( Hirai et al., 2025 ) . This could be common for these systems, as eccentric orbits allow for closer periastrons and therefore a larger amount of accretable matter ( Ercolino et al., 2026 ) . On the other hand, the oscillations in SN 2022esa were symmetric ( Maeda et al., 2026 ) ; if these are also due to binary accretion, then skewness is not necessarily universal. For simplicity, we mainly simulate the accretion-induced oscillations as a pure sinusoid. The search with λ = 1 \lambda=1 has difficulty recovering signals with T osc > 50 T_{\mathrm{osc}}>50 d (Fig. 5 , left), as P max P_{\mathrm{max}} is instead found at T recov < T osc T_{\mathrm{recov}}<T_{\mathrm{osc}} (Fig. 4 ). In contrast, the search with λ = 10 \lambda=10 performs comparatively better for these longer period oscillations but worse for the shorter period ones. As expected, signals with larger amplitudes A osc A_{\mathrm{osc}} and shorter delays Δ osc \Delta_{\mathrm{osc}} are more likely to be recovered. While we limited our simulations to A osc < 200 A_{\mathrm{osc}}<200 and Δ osc < 100 \Delta_{\mathrm{osc}}<100 d, it is clear that oscillation signals that are louder than this limit are more likely to be recovered, while delays longer than this are less likely to be recovered as fewer full oscillation cycles are observed. Of course, a longer observation duration t obs t_{\mathrm{obs}} would allow for scenarios with longer delays and periods to be explored. For the search with λ = 1 \lambda=1 , none of the rebrightening parameters had an effect on signal recovery (Fig. 17 ). In fact, when we reran the search on a set of simulated lightcurves without the rebrightening feature (i.e., SN and oscillations only), the fraction of recoverable signals remains the same. For the λ = 10 \lambda=10 search, the overall percentage of recoverable signals increased by 5 or 10% when the rebrightening features were removed. This indicates that the λ = 1 \lambda=1 spline is flexible enough to accommodate the rebrightening features while the λ = 10 \lambda=10 spline is moderately affected by them, and searches that use stiffer splines (e.g., to be more sensitive to longer period oscillations) will have to account for this by, e.g., excluding more early data. 4 Results 4.1 Observational gaps Approximately 10% of scheduled ZTF observations are canceled due to external reasons such as bad weather. When the lost observations are randomly distributed, the effect of this is minimal (Fig. 23 ): When we dropped a random 10% of observations, the the standard search with λ = 1 \lambda=1 was unable to recover only 1.1% of the previously recoverable signals. (With a more pessimistic 30% drop rate, 4.3% are no longer recoverable. For the search with λ = 10 \lambda=10 , the reduction in the recoverable signals is 1.3% and 6.1% for the 10% and 30% drop rates, respectively.) We will therefore apply a random 10% loss of observations to the searches on simulated data in this section. The power in the window function itself is shown by the shaded region. When there is no additional oscillatory signal (black curves), the periodogram shows no strong features. However, when an additional bright 5-day (blue) or 30-day (orange) oscillation is included, there is additional structure due to the interplay between the signal periods and the gap timescales. The vertical dotted lines mark f osc f_{\mathrm{osc}} for the two signals. In reality, the canceled observations are more likely to appear consecutively due to external conditions that span multiple days. These longer gaps would decrease the sensitivity to signals and increase the number of false alarms. In particular, multiple long gaps can add an additional timescale to the system and lead to more complex features in the periodograms. Fig. 6 illustrates this by comparing the periodograms for three lightcurves with the same observation dates, which are taken as the dates of the g g -band observations of SN 2018gf (to be discussed in Sec. 5.1 ). This is a SN with multiple long gaps in its lightcurve: a 56-day gap, a 27-day gap, and multiple gaps of 5-15 days. When the lightcurve contains no additional periodic signal (black curves), the periodogram does not show any strong features. However, for the lightcurves with additional periodic signals with T osc = 5 T_{\mathrm{osc}}=5 d (blue curves) or T osc = 30 T_{\mathrm{osc}}=30 d (red curves), the periodograms show more complex features and many high-power peaks beyond the ones expected at f osc f_{\mathrm{osc}} . The periodogram for the window function — calculated by applying the periodogram to a set of constant values at the observation times of the SN — only shows the peaks around 1/56 and 1/27, whereas the structure in the lightcurve periodograms comes from the combination of the multiple timescales. In this particular example, the 5-day period signal is recovered but the 30-day period signal is not; however, this is a specific example and does not necessarily generalize. The same will also occur when there is any short-duration variability, real or instrumental. Searches on real data will therefore have reduced sensitivity when structured gaps are present. 4.2 Total observation durations So far, we have assumed a very optimistic 200 days of observations after t 0 t_{0} for all SNe, but in reality, the majority of ZTF SNe are observed for a month before the planned schedule moves on to other parts of the sky, and only particularly bright or otherwise interesting SNe are observed longer. Shorter observation durations reduce the number of recoverable signals in multiple ways: The sensitivity reduces overall when fewer full cycles are observed, and the sensitivity to longer period signals and signals with longer delays Δ osc \Delta_{\mathrm{osc}} is especially reduced. In addition, with shorter observation durations — or, more precisely, a small number of data points N obs N_{\mathrm{obs}} — the periodogram peaks produced by noise fluctuations are taller.
